flows.name: AI chips up to the H200
flows.what: Data center accelerators up to the H200's level that were on sale in the United States when the January 2026 rule was published, such as the H100, the H200 and AMD's MI325X. Since 15 January 2026, license applications to export chips below 21,000 TPP and 6,500 GB/s of memory bandwidth from the United States to China or Macau are reviewed case by case. The exporter must certify, among other things, that US supply is sufficient and that a third party in the United States has tested the chips. BIS's summary of the rule limits it to chips on sale in the United States when it was published. The exporter must also certify that the chips sent to China and Macau add up to no more than half the computing power of the same chip shipped to US customers. A chip sold only in China, such as Nvidia's A800 or H800, cannot qualify, so applications for it still meet a presumption of denial. The H20 falls below the thresholds of ECCN 3A090, the US export category for advanced chips. It has needed a license for China since April 2025 because the US government told Nvidia so in a letter, under 15 CFR 744.23. The review policy that rule sets for buyers in China is a presumption of denial (744.23(d)).

Applications for other fabs, and for tools that a foreign maker sells free of US rules, are reviewed case by case.

flows.name: High-bandwidth memory
flows.route: US → China, including HBM made abroad
flows.what: Memory stacks with more than 2 GB per second of bandwidth per square millimeter, wherever they are made, including foreign stacks that the direct product rule brings under US control. A license is required to send them to Macau or Country Group D:5, the US list of arms-embargoed countries that includes China, and to send them anywhere for a firm headquartered there. Approval is presumed for buyers in China or Macau headquartered elsewhere, and denial for firms headquartered in D:5 or Macau, wherever the stacks go. License Exception HBM still lets an exporter in the US or in Country Group A:5, a group of close US partners, ship stacks below 3.3 GB per second per square millimeter without a license. The stacks must go directly to a packaging site for the designer that bought them.

flows.name: AI chips to the rest of the world
flows.route: US → D:1, D:4 and D:5, the UAE, five more countries, and D:5 or Macau firms
flows.what: Advanced AI chips, ECCN 3A090 except its memory entry 3A090.c, and the computers built from them, ECCN 4A090. Since 19 November 2026 a license is required to or within Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brazil and Thailand, under 15 CFR 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A)(1). Shipments there to a consignee or end user headquartered in the United States, or whose ultimate parent is, need no license if the exporter reports them to BIS each month. Under 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A)(2), a license is also required for destinations in Country Groups D:1, D:4 and D:5 that are not also in A:5 or A:6, and for the United Arab Emirates. Shipments to the approved entities in the UAE listed in supplement no. 8 to part 740 need no license. Under 15 CFR 744.23(a)(3), a license is required in any other destination when the items are for an entity headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau, or whose ultimate parent is. Under 15 CFR 744.24, a license is required in any destination when the shipper knows the items are bound for a data center that gives such entities access to more than 12,000,000 aggregate TPP, the sum of the TPP of the chips. Applications for the five countries, and for such data centers, are reviewed case by case. Applications for the other destinations in D:1 and D:4 and for the UAE meet a presumption of approval, and those for D:5, Macau and their firms a presumption of denial. The rule of 19 November 2026 also removed the AI Diffusion Rule of January 2025 from the regulations. That rule had required a license for the top band of these chips to or within any destination, and the Commerce Department said on 13 May 2025 it would rescind it. Compliance had been due on 15 May 2025, and the rule of 19 November 2026 says the AI Diffusion Rule was never enforced. BIS went on enforcing the license requirement for D:1, D:4 and D:5 destinations outside A:5 and A:6, and for firms headquartered in D:5 or Macau. The AI Diffusion Rule let exporters ship without a license to nineteen destinations, the United States and eighteen allies listed in supplement no. 5 to part 740, under License Exception AIA. License Exception LPP allowed up to 26,900,000 TPP a year per recipient elsewhere. The rule reviewed license applications for the nineteen with a presumption of approval, and those for other destinations the same way up to a cap of 790,000,000 TPP per country through 2027. Applications for D:5, Macau and their firms met a presumption of denial.
